facts.title: Discovered in radioactive dregs
facts.text: Radium was discovered in December 1898 by Marie and Pierre Curie, working in a leaky shed in Paris with leftover uranium ore called pitchblende from Joachimsthal in Bohemia. They noticed the ore was far more radioactive than its uranium content could explain, which pointed to an unknown element. To prove it existed, Marie processed several tonnes of ore to isolate just a fraction of a gram of radium chloride.

facts.title: Named for its rays
facts.text: The Curies named the element from the Latin word 'radius', meaning ray, because of the intense radiation it emits. Marie Curie even coined the word 'radioactivity' itself during this research. The discovery helped earn her two Nobel Prizes: Physics in 1903 (shared) and Chemistry in 1911 for isolating pure radium metal.

facts.title: It glows in the dark
facts.text: Radium emits enough energy that it makes nearby materials fluoresce, producing a faint blue-green glow without any external light source. The Curies described keeping glowing tubes of radium salts by their bedside and admiring their luminous beauty. This glow comes from the radiation exciting the surrounding air and any phosphors present, not from the radium giving off visible light directly.

facts.title: Heavier than its family
facts.text: Radium is the heaviest of the alkaline-earth metals, sitting at the bottom of Group 2 below barium, with atomic number 88. Like calcium and barium, it has two valence electrons and forms a +2 ion, so chemically it behaves much like its lighter relatives. Pure radium metal is silvery-white but quickly turns black when exposed to air as it reacts with nitrogen.

facts.title: Every atom is unstable
facts.text: Radium has no stable isotopes; every form of it is radioactive. The most common isotope, radium-226, has a half-life of about 1,600 years and decays by emitting an alpha particle. It is part of the natural decay chain of uranium-238, which is why radium is found wherever uranium ores occur in the Earth's crust.

facts.title: The deadly Radium Girls
facts.text: In the 1910s and 1920s, factory workers in the United States painted glow-in-the-dark watch and instrument dials with radium-based paint, often licking their brushes to a fine point. Many of these 'Radium Girls' developed severe bone damage, anemia, and cancers of the jaw and mouth. Their landmark lawsuits in the late 1920s helped establish modern labor safety rights and occupational health standards.

facts.title: It mimics calcium in bone
facts.text: Because radium chemically resembles calcium, the body mistakes it for calcium and deposits it in bones. There it irradiates surrounding tissue and bone marrow, which can cause cancers and blood disorders. This 'bone-seeking' behavior is exactly what made the radium dial painters so vulnerable to harm.

facts.title: A pioneer of cancer therapy
facts.text: Before safer alternatives existed, sealed radium needles and tubes were implanted near tumors to destroy cancerous cells with radiation, a technique called brachytherapy. This early form of radiotherapy saved lives and proved that radiation could fight as well as cause disease. Today radium has been almost entirely replaced by isotopes like cobalt-60 and iridium-192 that are easier and safer to handle.

facts.title: Glowing paint and quack cures
facts.text: In the early 20th century, radium was marketed in toothpaste, face creams, drinking water, and tonics promising health and vigor before its dangers were understood. The most infamous case was American socialite Eben Byers, who died in 1932 after drinking a radium tonic called Radithor, his jaw and bones destroyed. These tragedies pushed governments to regulate radioactive consumer products.

facts.title: Still fighting cancer today
facts.text: A modern medicine called Radium-223 dichloride, sold as Xofigo, was approved by the US FDA in 2013 to treat prostate cancer that has spread to the bones. Its calcium-like chemistry is now an advantage: it travels straight to bone tumors and delivers short-range alpha radiation that kills cancer cells while sparing nearby healthy tissue. This turns radium's old danger into a precisely targeted weapon.
